'''''Vaccinium myrtillus''''' is a [[holarctic]] species of [[shrub]] with edible fruit of blue color, known by the common names '''[[bilberry]]''', '''blaeberry''', and '''whortleberry'''.<ref name="nihgov" /> It is more precisely called '''common bilberry''' or '''blue whortleberry''' to distinguish it from other ''[[Vaccinium]]'' relatives.

==Description==
''Vaccinium myrtillus'' is a small [[deciduous]] shrub that grows {{Convert|4-20|in|cm|order=flip}} tall, heavily branched with upright, angular to narrow winged, green-colored branches that are glabrous. It grows [[rhizome]]s, creating extensive patches. The shrub can live up to 30 years, with roots reaching depths of up to {{Convert|1|m|ft|frac=2}}. It has light green [[leaves]] that turn red in autumn and are simple and alternate in arrangement.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=''Vaccinium myrtillus'' |url=https://www.fs.usda.gov/database/feis/plants/shrub/vacmyr/all.html |access-date=2022-09-13 |website=www.fs.usda.gov}}</ref> The leaves are {{Convert|1-3|cm|abbr=on|frac=8}} long and ovate to lanceolate or broadly elliptic in shape, with glandular to finely toothed margins;<ref name=":0" /> they are prominently veined on the lower surface.<ref name="tktimb">{{Cite book |last1=Turner |first1=Mark |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VLbAAwAAQBAJ |title=Trees & Shrubs of the Pacific Northwest |last2=Kuhlmann |first2=Ellen |date=2014 |publisher=[[Timber Press]] |isbn=978-1-60469-263-1 |edition=1st |location=Portland, OR |pages=180}}</ref> In winter, the foliage turns deep red and becomes deciduous.

Small, [[hermaphrodite]] flowers with thick [[Pedicel (botany)|stems]] (about {{convert|2–3|mm|disp=or|frac=16}} long) grow individually from the leaf axils and nod downward. These flowers, blooming from April to May, have crowns 4 to 6 mm long that are greenish to reddish. The small [[Sepal|calyx]] is fused with minimal lobes on the cup-shaped flower. The rounded, urn-shaped, white-to-pink petals<ref name="tktimb" /> have short, curved lobes. The 8–10 stamens are short, and the anthers are awned and horned. The four- or five-chambered ovary is inferior with a long style.

From July to September, the plants produce black-blue, flattened, round fruits with a diameter up to 1 cm.<ref name="tktimb" /> These multi-seeded berries have calyx remnants on the tip and a blue-gray frosted appearance. Rarely, forms with white, yellow, red, or reddish-spotted berries occur. The small, brownish seeds are crescent-shaped. This species differs from [[Vaccinium corymbosum|''V. corymbosum'']] in that its [[anthocyanin]]s, which produce color, are found in both the peel and the flesh. Its fruit [[persistence (botany)|persists]] for an average of 16.7 days, and bears an average of 25.3 seeds per fruit. Fruits average 85.4% water, and their [[dry matter|dry weight]] includes 31.1% [[carbohydrate]]s and 2.7% [[lipid]]s.{{sfn|Ehrlén|Eriksson|1991}}

The plant is [[diploid]], with a total of 24 [[chromosomes]].<ref name="y432">{{cite book | last=Oberdorfer | first=Erich | title=Pflanzensoziologische Exkursionsflora für Deutschland und angrenzende Gebiete | publisher=Ulmer | publication-place=Stuttgart | date=2001 | isbn=3-8001-3131-5 | language=de | page=732}}</ref><ref name="r875">{{cite web | title=Bilberry | website=GDV | url=https://www.vaccinium.org/crop/bilberry | access-date=2024-07-08}}</ref>

=== Chemistry ===
Bilberry and the related ''[[Vaccinium uliginosum|V. uliginosum]]'' both produce [[lignin]]s, in part because they are used as [[plant defense against herbivory|defensive chemicals]].<ref name="climate-change">{{cite journal |last1=Bidart-Bouzat |first1=M. Gabriela |last2=Imeh-Nathaniel |first2=Adebobola |year=2008 |title=Global Change Effects on Plant Chemical Defenses against Insect Herbivores |journal=Journal of Integrative Plant Biology |volume=50 |issue=11 |pages=1339–1354 |doi=10.1111/j.1744-7909.2008.00751.x |issn=1672-9072 |pmid=19017122 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2008JIPB...50.1339B }}</ref> Although many plants change their lignin production – usually to increase it – to handle the stresses of [[climate change]], lignin levels of both ''Vaccinium'' species appear to be unaffected.<ref name="climate-change" /> The leaves contain catechins, tannins, quinic acid, arbutin, chlorogenic acid, various glycosides, the fruits contain anthocyanins, [[pectin]], [[ursolic acid]], [[chlorogenic acid]], and [[ascorbic acid]].<ref name="c252">{{cite web |title=Vaccinium myrtillus |url=https://phytochem.nal.usda.gov/plant-vaccinium-myrtillus |access-date=2024-06-18 |website=Dr. Duke's Phytochemical and Ethnobotanical Databases}}</ref>

''V. myrtillus'' contains a high concentration of [[triterpene]]s which remain under laboratory research for their possible biological effects.<ref name="waxes">{{cite journal |last1=Szakiel |first1=Anna |last2=Pączkowski |first2=Cezary |last3=Pensec |first3=Flora |last4=Bertsch |first4=Christophe |year=2012 |title=Fruit cuticular waxes as a source of biologically active triterpenoids |journal=Phytochemistry Reviews |volume=11 |issue=2–3 |pages=263–284 |bibcode=2012PChRv..11..263S |doi=10.1007/s11101-012-9241-9 |issn=1568-7767 |pmc=3601259 |pmid=23519009 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Etymology ==
The genus ''Vaccinium'' has at least three theories as to its origin.<ref name="Small & Catling">{{Cite book |last1=Small |first1=Ernest |last2=Catling |first2=Paul M. |date=1999 |title=Canadian Medicinal Crops |url=https://archive.org/details/canadianmedicina0000smal |url-access=registration |location=Ottawa |publisher=NRC Research Press |isbn=978-0-660-17534-8 |oclc=70764249 |access-date=16 December 2025}}</ref><ref name="Hyam & Pankhurst">{{Cite book |last1=Hyam |first1=Roger |last2=Pankhurst |first2=Richard J. |author-link2=Richard Pankhurst (botanist) |date=1995 |title=Plants and Their Names: A Concise Dictionary |url=https://archive.org/details/plantstheirnames0000hyam |url-access=registration |location=Oxford, England |publisher=Oxford University Press; Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh |page=515 |isbn=978-0-19-866189-4 |oclc=30026609 |access-date=16 December 2025}}</ref> It might be taken from the Latin {{lang|la|vacca}} for cow with the idea it was named for cows eating the bushes, but it may be from {{lang|la|bacca}} the word for berry.<ref name="Small & Catling" /> The third theory is that is derives from the genus ''[[Hyacinthus]]''.<ref name="Hyam & Pankhurst" /> The species name refers to the resemblance of its leaves to that of [[common myrtle]].<ref name="Small & Catling" />

The name ''bilberry'' is primarily applied to ''Vaccinium myrtillus'',<ref name="OED Bilberry">{{Cite OED|Bilberry, N. |2755222901}}</ref> but is also an alternate name for the genus ''Vaccinium'' as a whole.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=VASCAN |last2=Acadia University |last3=Université de Montréal Biodiversity Centre |last4=University of Toronto Mississauga |last5=University of British Columbia |date=2025 |title=''Vaccinium'' Linnaeus – Database of Vascular Plants of Canada (VASCAN) |url=https://data.canadensys.net/vascan/taxon/1806 |website=Canadensys |language=en |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250215124107/https://data.canadensys.net/vascan/taxon/1806 |archive-date=15 February 2025 |access-date=16 December 2025}}</ref> The name bilberry appears to be an English borrowing from [[Old Norse]] being very similar to the [[Danish language|Danish]] {{lang|da|böllebær}}, used for the same plant.<ref name="OED Bilberry" /> The names ''whortleberry'',<ref>{{Cite OED|Whortleberry, N. |1044047444}}</ref> ''whortles'',<ref>{{Cite OED|Whortle, N. |2268755724}}</ref> and ''tracleberry'',<ref name="Small & Catling" /> are similarly generally applied to this species but are also sometimes used for other species or the genus.<ref name="Small & Catling" /> The name ''[[huckleberry]]'' generally means species in the related genus ''[[Gaylussacia]]'',<ref>{{Cite OED|Huckleberry, N. |1042837581}}</ref> but is also sometimes used to mean ''V. myrtillus'' or other species of the blueberry genus.<ref name="Small & Catling" />

The names ''myrtille'' and ''myrtle whortleberry'' are preferred in Canada specifically mean this plant species.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=VASCAN |last2=Acadia University |last3=Université de Montréal Biodiversity Centre |last4=University of Toronto Mississauga |last5=University of British Columbia |date=2025 |title=''Vaccinium myrtillus'' Linnaeus – Database of Vascular Plants of Canada (VASCAN) |url=https://data.canadensys.net/vascan/taxon/5574?lang=en |website=Canadensys |language=en-ca |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230730070951/https://data.canadensys.net/vascan/taxon/5574?lang=en |archive-date=30 July 2023 |access-date=16 December 2025}}</ref>

Regional names include ''blaeberry'' (in Scotland), {{lang|gd|braoileag}} (in [[Scottish Gaelic]]),<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sinclair |first=Fiona |date=June 2001 |title=A site devoted to ''Vaccinium Myrtillus'' and the Scottish environment. Blaeberry in Scots, Braoileag in Gaelic, Vaccinium Myrtillus in Latin. |url=https://blaeberry.org/ |access-date=2025-10-11 |website=Project Blaeberry, a site devoted to Vaccinium Myrtillus and the Scottish environment. |language=en-GB}}</ref> ''urts'' or ''hurts'' (Cornwall and Devon),<ref>{{cite book|last=Phillipps|first=K. C.|title=A Glossary of the Cornish Dialect|year=1993|publisher=Tabb House|location=Padstow|isbn=0-907018-91-2|page=57}}</ref> ''hurtleberry'',<ref name="grin">{{GRIN | access-date = 12 December 2017}} citing Wiersema, J. (1992), ''The new Royal Horticultural Society dictionary of gardening''</ref> ''myrtleberry'',<ref>{{Cite web|title=Bilberry, Blaeberry, Whortleberry, Whinberry, Windberry, Myrtle Berry, Vaccinium myrtillus|url=https://www.wildfooduk.com/edible-wild-plants/bilberry/|access-date=2020-07-31|website=Wild Food UK|language=en-GB}}</ref> ''wimberry'', ''whinberry'',<ref>{{Cite web|title=Whinberry Gin Liqueur|url=https://www.kirkwooddistillery.co.uk/whinberry|access-date=2025-07-12|website=Kirkwood Distillery|language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Whinberry Picking – 'A Cautionary Tale'|url=https://www.baldhiker.com/whinberry-picking-a-cautionary-tale/|website=Bald Hiker|language=en-GB}}</ref> ''winberry'',<ref name="henley">Henley, Jon. [https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2008/jun/09/foodanddrink.food Bilberries: the true taste of northern England], The Guardian, Monday 9 June 2008</ref> and ''fraughan''.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.tearma.ie/Search.aspx?term=fraoch%C3%A1n |title=''Fraughan'' is an anglicisation of the Irish word ''Fraochán'' (or ''heather fruit'', as the plant is often found growing with heather) |publisher= téarma.ie}}</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==
''Vaccinium myrtillus'' is a [[Holarctic realm|Holarctic]] species native to almost every country in Europe, north and central Asia, Japan, Greenland, Western Canada, and the Western United States. Within Europe it is only absent from [[Sardinia]], [[Sicily]], the European portion of [[Turkey]], [[Crete]], the [[Aegean Islands]], [[Cyprus]], [[Crimea]], and southern [[European Russia]].<ref name="POWO">{{cite POWO |id=30006039-2 |title=''Vaccinium myrtillus'' L. |access-date=27 June 2024}}</ref> It occurs in the acidic soils of [[heath]]s, boggy [[Barren vegetation|barrens]], [[moorland]]s, degraded meadows, open forests at the base of pine and mountain spruce forests, and parklands, slopes, and [[moraine]]s at elevations up to {{Convert|2350|m|abbr=on}}.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=200016692 |title=''Vaccinium myrtillus'' Linnaeus |publisher=Flora of North America |date= |accessdate=2021-09-21}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://plants.usda.gov/home/plantProfile?symbol=VAMY2 |title=''Vaccinium myrtillus'' L. |publisher=USDA Plants Database |date= |accessdate=2021-09-21}}</ref>

== Toxicity ==
Consuming the leaves may be unsafe.<ref name="nihgov" />

== Uses ==
[[File:Hands scooping up fresh bilberries picked in Tuntorp.jpg|thumb|Bilberries have dark red juice that stains hands.]]
[[File:Llusi duon bach.jpg|thumb|Bilberries]]

=== Fruit ===
The berry is edible.<ref name="tktimb" /> The fruits will stain hands, teeth and tongue deep blue or purple while eating and so it was traditionally used as a [[dye]] for food and clothes in Britain.<ref>{{cite web |title=Make Traditional Dyes – Bilberry Dye |url=http://www.barleyhall.org.uk/MakeTraditionalDyes.asp |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120421235953/http://www.barleyhall.org.uk/MakeTraditionalDyes.asp |archive-date=2012-04-21 |website=Barley Hall |publisher=[[York Archaeological Trust]], [[Arts Council England]] and [[VisitEngland]]}}</ref>

In cooking, the bilberry fruit is commonly used for pies, tarts and flans, cakes, jams, [[muffin]]s, cookies, sauces, [[syrup]]s, juices, and candies.<ref name="nihgov" />

Although bilberries are in high demand by consumers in Northern Europe, the berries are harvested in the wild without any cultivation. Some authors state that opportunities exist to improve the crop if cultivated using common agricultural practices.<ref name="Nestby">{{cite journal |last1=Nestby |first1=Rolf |last2=Percival |first2=D. |last3=Martinussen |first3=Inger S. |last4=Opstad |first4=Nina |last5=Rohloff |first5=Jens |date=January 2011 |title=The European Blueberry (''Vaccinium myrtillus'' L .) and the Potential for Cultivation. A Review |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220005144 |journal=The European Journal of Plant Science and Biotechnology |s2cid=52997599}}</ref>

===Dietary supplement===
Bilberry [[dietary supplement]]s are marketed in some countries, although there is no evidence these products have any effect on health or diseases.<ref name="nihgov">{{cite web|url=https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/bilberry |title=Bilberry|publisher=National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, US National Institutes of Health |date=1 November 2024|accessdate=7 June 2026}}</ref> ''Vaccinium myrtillus'' has been used for centuries in [[traditional medicine]], particularly in traditional [[Austria]]n medicine as a tea or liqueur in attempts to treat various disorders.<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Vogl S, Picker P, Mihaly-Bison J, Fakhrudin N, Atanasov AG, Heiss EH, Wawrosch C, Reznicek G, Dirsch VM, Saukel J, Kopp B | doi = 10.1016/j.jep.2013.06.007 |date=2013-03-25 |pmid=23770053 |volume=149 |title=Ethnopharmacological in vitro studies on Austria's folk medicine--an unexplored lore in vitro anti-inflammatory activities of 71 Austrian traditional herbal drugs |journal=J Ethnopharmacol | issue = 3 |pages=750–71 |pmc=3791396}}</ref>

=== Leaves ===
In traditional medicine, the (potentially toxic) leaves were mainly used for treating skin disorders.<ref name="nihgov" />
